A Utah mother pushes past pain and fear on the ninja course—turning personal loss into strength, both in competition and on canvas. Known as the “Art Ninja,” Jenedy Paige balances elite obstacle course competition with a thriving art career—fueled by faith, family and loss.
A Utah mother pushes past pain and fear on the ninja course—turning personal loss into strength, both in competition and on canvas. Known as the “Art Ninja,” Jenedy Paige balances elite obstacle course competition with a thriving art career—fueled by faith, family and loss.
Paige spoke with ARC Salt Lake about the journey that shaped her—and the purpose that keeps her moving forward.

“There’s like a space in time where you’re levitating. It’s awesome,” Paige said about flying through the air in the obstacle course where she trains.
“You’re like, ‘Well, I’m a mom. I’ve run a 5K, so we’re like the same,’” she said.
“The reason I kept coming back was that I surprised myself,” Paige said. “Things that I thought were impossible, after trying a bunch of times and falling on my face – eventually I accomplished the thing that was impossible.”
“I tore my shoulder in 2020 and I’ve broken my nose twice,” she said.
“They actually did air my run last season, and I’m going to be aired again in June – and then I’ll compete again in September,” she said.
Her journey has not come without unimaginable pain. Almost 15 years ago, her 3-year-old son, Victory, died in a drowning incident.
“My son’s name is Victory, so how can you not want to exceed at something when you have an angel in heaven cheering you on,” Paige said.
“The title of this painting is ‘His Strength is mine,’ because it’s the strength that I feel that comes from my faith and also the strength that I feel from my son on the other side.”
Paige specializes in portrait paintings at her Pleasant Grove studio. Her work – exquisite and so real – is in high demand.
“You go from big, dynamic movements to little, teeny, tiny brushes,” she said.
Paige has an online store, does custom paintings for clients and has a gallery full of depictions of strong women.
“I just wanted to, kind of, shine a light on that – of how important it is that we have strong women in our communities and in our lives and the good that they do,” she said.
Among her painting are depictions of women breaking down walls, pushing the limits and healing from hurt.
“I think if we sent a little less time on our phones and just took maybe 15 minutes a day to write, the world would definitely be a better place,” Paige said.
